newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE urged to play role in Croatian enclave.
newsitem.headline: OSCE urged to play role in Croatian enclave.

text.p: A senior U.N. official called on Europe's top security forum on Thursday to send monitors to Croatia's last separatist enclave, Eastern Slavonia, to maintain peace there when the current U.N. mandate runs out.

Jacques Klein, the U.S. diplomat heading the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), told the OSCE that the future of the Serb-run enclave must become a European, rather than a global, responsibility.

"If the OSCE is to fulfil the role it sees for itself in Europe...it must be prepared to take the leading role in maintaining security, cooperation and stability in Eastern Slavonia," Klein said in a speech to the permanent council of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

Eastern Slavonia, a fertile Danube valley plain, is due to come back under Croatian rule after elections on April 13, in a peaceful end to six years of ethnic conflict punctuated by the government's reconquest of two other Serb enclaves.
Serbs took control of the region in 1991, after rebelling against Croatia's bid for independence from former Yugoslavia.
The U.N. military mandate will expire on July 15. A reduced U.N. mission will stay in the area until January 1998.
Klein said it was vital to have an OSCE presence of around 200 observers for at least two years after that.

"It is absolutely essential because we made promises to the people of the region. We have told 100,000 Serbs 'we have guaranteed your future if you stay here'," he told a news briefing at the headquarters of the 54-nation OSCE in Vienna.
"The challenge is one I think they (the OSCE) are prepared to accept," Klein said, noting Russia, the United States and the European Union had appeared to favour his proposal.

The Croatian government, in a letter of intent to the Security Council, promised Serbs a wide-ranging package including representation in the national parliament, senior positions in five ministries, at least 700 Serb police posts and local educational and cultural autonomy.
But Klein said the minority Serb population of some 120,000 remained distrustful of the Croatian pledges and were subject to intimidation from local agitators.
Between 15,000 and 20,000 of them could be expected to return to Serbia, he noted.
"Some are war criminals, some have guilty consciences, some have money and business on the other side and some cannot see themselves as Serb nationalists living in a Croatian state."
Klein said the forthcoming elections were the key to peaceful reintegration.
"This will be a U.N. success story and probably one of the only places where we effect some kind of multi-ethnic return," he said.
